claims.reason: The quotes show that the recommended minimum interval before bedtime differs by source and product (NHS tea or coffee versus the meta-analysis coffee versus pre-workout supplement), which supports that there is no single interval for everything. No snapshot states in so many words that no universal limit exists, and neither snapshot describes differences between people.

The clock time 14:00 is the editors' illustrative example of the single cut-off hour the item declines to offer (see the title). It is not a figure of any source: no snapshot mentions it or any clock time. Listed here so that a person checks it; it is not hidden as a source figure and no calculation is claimed.

scope_gaps.note: The sources give intervals measured back from bedtime that differ by source and product. None of them describes variation between people or advises against a single cut-off; the NHS page itself gives one interval for tea and coffee.
The snapshots name coffee, tea and a pre-workout supplement, and the NHS page lists caffeine among common causes of insomnia. Other caffeine sources are not covered.
The abstract does not describe how the cut-off intervals were derived from the pooled data. The sentence does not claim a method.
The abstract does not give the dose, timing or population behind the pooled reduction. The sentence claims none, but a reader might assume it applies to any dose and timing.
The abstract states the intervals as minimum intervals ('at least') for avoiding a reduction in total sleep time; the sentence omits 'co najmniej'.
The description fits the meta-analysis only. The other cited source is an NHS patient information page, not a quantitative synthesis, and a reader might assume the whole item rests on one.
The sources give only intervals before bedtime. No snapshot mentions clock times such as the one named in the sentence, so a clock-time cut-off follows only if a bedtime is assumed.
